overview:
The kings west of the Jordan lose heart when they hear of the crossing. At that time the LORD tells Joshua to make flint knives and circumcise Israel again: the men who left Egypt had been circumcised, but those born in the wilderness had not. The place is called Gilgal, because the LORD has “rolled away the reproach of Egypt.” Israel keeps the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month, eats grain of the land the next day, and the manna stops. Near Jericho, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword, the captain of the LORD's host, who tells him to take off his shoe, for the ground is holy.

Look at the order. Before a single battle, Israel's fighting men are left unable to fight until they heal (v. 8), a feast is kept within sight of Jericho, and the commander is sent barefoot. The land is entered first through covenant and worship.

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Joshua, with the account of his death added by Eleazar and Phinehas; many scholars see the book as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Joshua's lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The days after the crossing on the tenth of the first month (4:19), with Passover on the fourteenth (v. 10), forty years after the Exodus (v. 6): about 1406 BC by 1 Kings 6:1, or about 1210 BC on the later date.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Gilgal on the plains of Jericho (vv. 9–10); the encounter with the captain happens “by Jericho” (v. 13).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Exodus 3:5 (holy ground at the bush); Exodus 12 and Numbers 9:1–5 (earlier Passovers); Exodus 16:35 (manna until the borders of Canaan).

hermeneutics:
Gods handed swords to kings before battle. In Merneptah's account of his Libyan war, carved at Karnak (c. 1208 BC), the king dreams that a statue of Ptah stands before him and holds out a sword, saying “Take thou (it),” and telling him to banish fear. Ashurbanipal of Assyria (7th century BC) records a seer's dream before his war with Elam in which Ishtar of Arbela appears with quivers and a bow, holding “a sharp sword” unsheathed for battle, and promises to go wherever the king goes. Joshua's visitor also stands before battle with his sword drawn (v. 13), and Joshua asks the obvious question: are you for us? The answer is “Nay.” The captain hands over no sword and takes no side. He comes as commander of the LORD's host, and Joshua falls on his face and takes off his shoe.

Circumcision marked peoples, and Egyptians noticed it. The same Karnak inscription counts the Libyan dead by their uncircumcised members, carried off as trophies, while for the Ekwesh, a sea people “who had no foreskins,” the scribes counted hands instead. Egypt circumcised, and it recorded who did not. Verses 4–7 explain that a whole generation born in the wilderness had grown up without the mark their fathers carried out of Egypt. The rite at Gilgal restores it before any fighting, and it leaves the army in pain for days (v. 8) beside a walled city.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence through three acts of preparation before Jericho.

rows.text: Passover and the end of manna

notes: **Rolling:** v. 9 explains the name by a pun: the LORD has “rolled away” (*galal*) the reproach, and *Gilgal* sounds like it.
**Circumcise:** the verb comes 8 times in vv. 2–8, with a long explanation (vv. 4–7) that is unusual in the book.

**Holy ground:** v. 15 repeats the words to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:5): loose the shoe, for “the place whereon thou standest is holy.” Joshua, magnified like Moses in 4:14, now meets God as Moses did.

Chapter 5 closes the book's first section, the entry into the land (chapters 1–5). Verse 1 looks back to the crossing, and the circumcision, the Passover, and the end of the manna prepare the people; the captain prepares their leader. His message seems to run on into 6:2–5, where the LORD gives the plan for Jericho, so the chapter break may cut one scene in two.
**Backward and forward:** the Passover at Gilgal answers the one kept at Sinai (Numbers 9:5). Gilgal later becomes a shrine the prophets condemn (Hosea 4:15; Amos 4:4).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote to v. 15 points to a revelation naming Far West, Missouri, as a gathering place for the Saints. The Lord calls it a holy and consecrated land, “for the ground upon which thou standest is holy.” The words given to Moses at the bush and to Joshua outside Jericho are applied to a Latter-day Saint city.

Why had the wilderness generation gone uncircumcised (vv. 5–7)? The Talmud offers two answers: the travelers were too weary, or the north wind, needed for healing, never blew in those forty years, either as a punishment after the spies or so the clouds of glory would not scatter. On “the second time” (v. 2), Rabba bar Yitzhak says some who had been circumcised in Abraham's manner needed the rite completed as the law given at Sinai required.

What was “the reproach of Egypt” (v. 9)? Rashi, following Moses ha-Darshan, says the Egyptians had taunted Israel with a star called Ra'ah, a sign of blood, which they claimed would overpower them in the wilderness (Exodus 10:10). The blood they foresaw, he says, was the blood of circumcision, and when it was shed at Gilgal the taunt was rolled away.

Josephus says nothing about the circumcision at Gilgal. He does explain the name: the camp was called Gilgal, which “denotes liberty,” because once across the Jordan the Hebrews counted themselves free of what they had suffered in Egypt and the wilderness. He has the manna fail as they began to reap the Canaanites' ripe grain.

Both explain why the manna stopped. Pseudo-Philo says that after Moses died the manna ceased, because God gave three gifts for the sake of three persons: the well for Miriam, the pillar of cloud for Aaron, and the manna for Moses; when the three died, the gifts were taken away. A baraita in the Talmud gives the same three gifts and merits, which numbers-020 cites for Miriam's well; here the manna's end in v. 12 is tied to Moses' death.

The Talmud asks how Joshua could bow to an unknown figure at night, and answers that a demon does not speak the name of God in vain. The captain, it says, came to rebuke Joshua for neglecting the afternoon offering and, that night, the study of Torah; “now am I come” shows the second fault was the graver. Rashi identifies the captain as the angel Michael, who had offered to go with Moses and been refused (Exodus 33:15).

The Aramaic Targum keeps the scene but changes the visitor's title. When Joshua asks whether he has come to help Israel, he answers that he is an angel sent from before the LORD, and it is this angel who tells Joshua to remove his shoe. The Targum also says the generation of v. 6 died because they did not accept the Memra, the Word, of the LORD.

Justin makes two uses of this chapter. To prove that the one who appeared to the patriarchs was the Son, begotten before all creatures, he quotes vv. 13–15 in full: Joshua worships the captain of the Lord's host. And he reads the “knives of stone” of v. 2 as Christ's words, by which those who entered the holy land with the true Joshua are circumcised in heart from idols of stone.

Lactantius lists v. 2 among prophecies that circumcision of the flesh would give way to circumcision of the heart. He notices that the text says the Lord spoke “unto Jesus,” not to the prophet himself, and takes it as addressed to Christ, the true Jesus. He adds that Moses had renamed Auses as Jesus when he chose him to lead against Amalek.

Describing Paula's pilgrimage, Jerome has her look on the camp of Gilgal and the hill of the foreskins, “suggestive of the mystery of the second circumcision,” and he cites Paul's circumcision of the heart (Romans 2:28–29). The place named in v. 3 had become a stop on the pilgrim road.

Eusebius places Gilgal east of old Jericho toward the Jordan. There, he says, Joshua circumcised the people and kept the Passover, eating wheat for the first time after the manna ceased, and the tent of witness stood. The deserted site, two miles from Jericho, was still held sacred by people of the region, and under “the hill of the foreskins” he notes the stones from the Jordan shown nearby.

The Septuagint of vv. 4–6 differs from the Hebrew and is not used. Ishtar of Arbela's oracles to Esarhaddon (genesis-015) are a different text from Ashurbanipal's dream here.
